sentences: 1,2-Dichlorobenzene (CASRN: 95-50-1; DTXSID: DTXSID6020430; PubChem CID: 7239; EC Number: 202-425-9) is a chlorinated aromatic hydrocarbon with the molecular formula C₆H₄Cl₂ and a molecular weight of 147.0 g/mol [1].
The compound has been characterized as a hepatotoxic agent, consistent with hepatic bioactivation of reactive intermediates [1].
The compound has been identified as a hepatotoxic agent, and liver injury represents a principal target organ effect observed in experimental animal studies [1][2].

It is produced industrially by the chlorination of benzene or monochlorobenzene in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst, or alternatively via the Sandmeyer procedure from the appropriate chloroaniline precursor; these processes yield mixtures of ortho-, meta-, and para-dichlorobenzene isomers, which are subsequently separated [2].

The compound serves as a chemical intermediate in the synthesis of 3,4-dichloroaniline, dyes, herbicides, and pharmaceuticals, and functions as a solvent, heat transfer liquid, degreasing agent, paint solvent, paint remover, cylinder lubricant, and a solvent for waxes, gums, resins, tars, rubber, oils, and asphalts [2].

It is also employed as a deodorant and, historically, as an insecticide and soil fumigant, although its pesticide registrations in the United States have been cancelled and no currently registered pesticide products contain this substance [2].
Industrial products incorporating 1,2-dichlorobenzene include metal degreasing formulations and paint solvent preparations [2].

Technical-grade material typically contains 70–85% of the ortho-isomer, with the remainder consisting of meta- and para-dichlorobenzene isomers, trace chlorobenzene, and trichlorobenzene; pure-grade material contains greater than 99.8% of the ortho-isomer [2].

Human exposure may occur in occupational settings among chemical manufacturing plant operators, metal degreasing workers, paint formulators, and laboratory personnel through inhalation of vapors and dermal contact with the liquid [2].

Environmental exposure pathways include volatilization from industrial waste streams into ambient air, leaching from contaminated soil into groundwater, and adsorption to sediments in surface water bodies receiving industrial effluents [2].

Authoritative threshold limit value (TLV) documentation from the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists (ACGIH) was not available for review at the time of this writing; the relevant ACGIH documentation requires a subscription and specific values could not be confirmed from the data sources consulted [2].
1,2-Dichlorobenzene can be absorbed into the body by inhalation, through the skin, and by ingestion [2].
Inhalation represents the primary route of occupational exposure, given the compound's vapor pressure of 1.4 mm Hg at 25 °C, which supports meaningful volatilization under ambient conditions [2].

Following absorption, the compound is distributed to tissues throughout the body; consistent with its lipophilic character, distribution to adipose tissue and highly perfused organs, including the liver and kidneys, is anticipated [2].

Metabolism proceeds primarily via cytochrome P450-mediated oxidation, yielding reactive arene oxide intermediates and phenolic metabolites, including 3,4-dichlorophenol and 3,4-dichlorocatechol, which may be further conjugated with glucuronic acid or sulfate prior to excretion [2].
Excretion occurs predominantly via the urine as conjugated metabolites, with a smaller fraction eliminated through exhalation as unchanged parent compound or carbon dioxide [2].

The acute toxicological effects of 1,2-dichlorobenzene in humans and experimental animals include irritation of the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract following inhalation or dermal contact, as well as central nervous system depression at high exposure concentrations [2].
The compound has been identified as a hepatotoxic agent, and liver injury represents a principal target organ effect observed in experimental animal studies [1][2].
Chronic toxicity data sufficient to characterize lifetime health risks from prolonged exposure were similarly not available from the sources consulted [2][3].

The mechanism of toxicity of 1,2-dichlorobenzene is understood to involve cytochrome P450-mediated bioactivation to reactive arene oxide intermediates, which may covalently bind to cellular macromolecules, including proteins and DNA, thereby initiating cytotoxic and potentially genotoxic events [2].

Oxidative stress resulting from the generation of reactive oxygen species during metabolic activation is considered a contributing mechanism, particularly in the liver, where bioactivation is most active [2].
The phenolic and catechol metabolites produced during oxidative metabolism may undergo further redox cycling, amplifying oxidative damage to hepatic and renal tissues [2].
Glutathione depletion has been proposed as a secondary mechanism by which reactive intermediates overwhelm cellular antioxidant defenses, leading to lipid peroxidation and cell death [2].

In the domain of hazard identification, subchronic toxicity data characterizing effects following repeated intermediate-duration exposures are absent from the sources reviewed, representing a gap relevant to the assessment of occupational and repeated consumer exposure scenarios [2][3].

By contrast, exposure characterization is relatively well-supported: occupational exposure limits (OSHA PEL and NIOSH REL) are established [4][5], industrial and consumer uses are documented [2], and environmental fate and transport data are available [2].

Absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) data are also available at a qualitative level from the ATSDR Toxicological Profile, though quantitative pharmacokinetic parameters are incompletely characterized [2].

No maximum contaminant level (MCL) or maximum contaminant level goal (MCLG) under the Safe Drinking Water Act has been identified for 1,2-dichlorobenzene in the data sources reviewed for this report [3].

The EPA Integrated Risk Information System (IRIS) assessment for 1,2-dichlorobenzene was not accessible at the time of this writing due to a system error; accordingly, no oral reference dose (RfD), critical study NOAEL, or associated uncertainty factor could be confirmed from IRIS records [3].
Chronic toxicity data sufficient to characterize lifetime health risks from prolonged exposure were similarly not available from the sources consulted [2][3].
EPA, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), or other regulatory bodies was identified in the data sources reviewed for this report [3].

In the domain of hazard identification, subchronic toxicity data characterizing effects following repeated intermediate-duration exposures are absent from the sources reviewed, representing a gap relevant to the assessment of occupational and repeated consumer exposure scenarios [2][3].
Chronic toxicity data sufficient to support characterization of lifetime health risks are likewise unavailable, precluding a complete assessment of long-term exposure consequences [3].

No authoritative cancer classification has been identified from EPA, IARC, or other bodies, leaving the carcinogenic potential of 1,2-dichlorobenzene uncharacterized and preventing a weight-of-evidence determination [3].

In the domain of dose-response assessment, no oral reference dose (RfD) was confirmed from IRIS records due to a system access error at the time of this writing; without an established RfD, NOAEL, or point of departure from a critical study, health-based oral exposure limits and drinking water guidelines cannot be derived from first principles, and benchmark dose modeling or read-across from structurally related dichlorobenzene isomers may be required as interim approaches [3].

In the domain of risk characterization, no drinking water MCL or MCLG has been identified for 1,2-dichlorobenzene, meaning that environmental contamination of drinking water sources cannot be evaluated against an enforceable federal standard [3].
The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) has established a permissible exposure limit (PEL) for 1,2-dichlorobenzene of 50 ppm (300 mg/m³) as a ceiling value under Table Z-1 [4].

By contrast, exposure characterization is relatively well-supported: occupational exposure limits (OSHA PEL and NIOSH REL) are established [4][5], industrial and consumer uses are documented [2], and environmental fate and transport data are available [2].

entries.title: Rutaecarpine Protects against Acetaminophen-Induced Acute Liver Injury in Mice by Activating Antioxidant Enzymes

sentences: The induction of CYP2E1 alongside HMOX1 is mechanistically coherent with reactive oxygen species generation during halogenated aromatic metabolism, which may trigger downstream heme oxygenase-mediated cytoprotection [6][7].

CYP2E1, supported by 14 publications, is a well-characterized mediator of halogenated compound bioactivation; its induction is consistent with oxidative metabolite generation and has been linked to downstream HMOX1 co-induction in models of chemical hepatotoxicity [6][10].

Confidence in the mechanistic interpretation of the 1,2-DCB cardiac transcriptomic response is highest for the oxidative stress and xenobiotic metabolism signatures, which are supported by multiple consensus genes (HMOX1, CYP2E1, SRXN1, TXNRD1) with strong cross-study literature concordance [8][9][6].
The upregulation of canonical NRF2 target genes NQO1 and GCLC is consistent with an adaptive cellular response to electrophilic or oxidative insult generated during 1,2-DCB biotransformation [6].
The liver enrichment is consistent with the known hepatic biotransformation of 1,2-DCB via CYP2E1 and the shared phase II detoxification machinery between liver and kidney [21][6].

Both genes are well-established indicators of electrophilic and oxidative stress-driven NRF2 activation, and their upregulation in the kidney is consistent with the biotransformation of 1,2-DCB to reactive intermediates capable of activating the KEAP1/NRF2 axis [6][9].

Confidence in the biological interpretation of the 1,2-DCB renal transcriptomic response is high for the NRF2-mediated oxidative stress and xenobiotic metabolism signatures, given the convergent evidence from pathway enrichment, GO term analysis, BMD ordering, and the extensive multi-study literature support for NQO1, GCLC, SRXN1, CYP2E1, CAT, and BAX as consensus response genes [8][6][24].

CYP2E1, a cytochrome P450 isoform known to bioactivate halogenated aromatic compounds and generate reactive oxygen species, was upregulated and appeared in the metabolic and arachidonic acid metabolism pathways; its induction is mechanistically plausible given the role of CYP2E1 in the oxidative metabolism of chlorinated benzenes [6].

statements: Rutaecarpine protects against acetaminophen-induced acute liver injury in mice by activating antioxidant enzymes
Rutaecarpine pretreatment decreases serum ALT/AST activities and hepatic malondialdehyde content, prevents glutathione depletion, inhibits CYP2E1 expression, and reduces inflammatory cytokines

entries.title: Heteromeric complex formation between human cytochrome P450 CYP1A1 and heme oxygenase-1.

sentences: The induction of CYP2E1 alongside HMOX1 is mechanistically coherent with reactive oxygen species generation during halogenated aromatic metabolism, which may trigger downstream heme oxygenase-mediated cytoprotection [6][7].

POR, which encodes NADPH-cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase, was also responsive and has been shown to catalyze lipid peroxidation during ferroptotic cell death [11], and its co-expression with HMOX1 in the context of CYP450 complex formation [7] suggests potential for amplified oxidative injury in cardiac tissue.

statements: CYP1A1 forms a stable complex with HO-1 that is further stabilized in the presence of POR.
The interaction between CYP1A1 and HO-1 affects their functional characteristics, altering Km values but not Vmaxapp.

entries.title: Biomarkers of NRF2 signalling: Current status and future challenges

sentences: Concurrently, response to xenobiotic stimulus (GO:0009410; FDR = 8.90 × 10⁻⁵) was enriched across 15 genes including CYP2E1, HMOX1, MGST1, TXNRD1, and SRXN1, the majority of which were upregulated, consistent with activation of the NRF2 antioxidant response pathway [8][9].

Organ signature analysis indicated that the cardiac gene expression profile bore greatest resemblance to signatures from hepatic Kupffer cells, monocytes/macrophages, and renal tubular epithelium, driven predominantly by HMOX1 enrichment, which is consistent with the known broad inducibility of heme oxygenase-1 across stress-responsive cell types [8].

HMOX1 upregulation is a well-established indicator of NRF2 pathway activation and oxidative stress, and HMOX1, SRXN1, and TXNRD1 have been identified as robust NRF2 activity biomarkers across multiple cell types [8][9].

Confidence in the mechanistic interpretation of the 1,2-DCB cardiac transcriptomic response is highest for the oxidative stress and xenobiotic metabolism signatures, which are supported by multiple consensus genes (HMOX1, CYP2E1, SRXN1, TXNRD1) with strong cross-study literature concordance [8][9][6].
Key NRF2-associated genes — GCLC, NQO1, SRXN1, GPX3, and CAT — were represented across these terms, consistent with activation of the NRF2/ARE antioxidant response pathway [8].

Among the individual dose-responsive genes, NQO1 and GCLC emerged as the most sensitive and biologically informative markers of 1,2-DCB renal exposure, with BMD values at the lower end of the observed range and strong literature support as canonical NRF2 pathway biomarkers across multiple cell types and tissues [8][22].
SRXN1, a sulfiredoxin and additional NRF2 target, was also among the responsive genes, further supporting engagement of the antioxidant response program [8][23].

Confidence in the biological interpretation of the 1,2-DCB renal transcriptomic response is high for the NRF2-mediated oxidative stress and xenobiotic metabolism signatures, given the convergent evidence from pathway enrichment, GO term analysis, BMD ordering, and the extensive multi-study literature support for NQO1, GCLC, SRXN1, CYP2E1, CAT, and BAX as consensus response genes [8][6][24].

The ferroptosis pathway was represented by a complete five-gene set (GCLC, GCLM, GPX4, HMOX1, TP53), all upregulated, consistent with an adaptive cytoprotective response to lipid peroxidation stress [8].

These genes were upregulated across a BMD range of approximately 134–241 ppm and are well-established transcriptional targets of KEAP1-NRF2 signaling activated by electrophilic and oxidative insults [8].

GCLC, GCLM, HMOX1, NQO1, SRXN1, and TXNRD1 have been validated as robust NRF2 activity biomarkers across multiple cell types and species [8, 9], lending high confidence to the interpretation that 1,2-DCB activates hepatic NRF2 signaling in a dose-dependent manner.

GPX4, a phospholipid hydroperoxide glutathione peroxidase critical for suppressing ferroptosis, was upregulated with a BMD within the ferroptosis pathway cluster (median ~165 ppm), and its co-induction with GCLC, GCLM, and HMOX1 suggests that lipid peroxidation is an early hepatic stress signal following 1,2-DCB exposure [8].

The predominant upregulation of genes within these pathways — particularly the NRF2-associated antioxidant response genes GCLC, NQO1, SRXN1, and TXNRD1 — is consistent with an adaptive cellular response to oxidative stress induced by 1,2-DCB metabolism [8].

NQO1, a well-established NRF2 target gene and robust biomarker of NRF2 pathway activation across multiple cell types [8], was similarly upregulated and co-enriched with GCLC, SRXN1, and TXNRD1 across multiple GO terms and pathways, collectively constituting a canonical NRF2 transcriptional signature [8, 9].

statements: GCLC, GCLM, HMOX1, NQO1, SRXN1 and TXNRD1 are robust markers for NRF2 activity across multiple cell types.
There is a need for consensus on the most relevant set of genes/proteins that best represent NRF2 activity in different contexts.

entries.title: Binankadsurin A from Kadsura coccinea Fruits Ameliorates Acetaminophen-Induced Liver Injury Through Inhibiting Oxidative Stress by Keap1/Nrf2/HO-1 Pathway

sentences: CYP2E1, supported by 14 publications, is a well-characterized mediator of halogenated compound bioactivation; its induction is consistent with oxidative metabolite generation and has been linked to downstream HMOX1 co-induction in models of chemical hepatotoxicity [6][10].

statements: Binankadsurin A (BKA) reduces acetaminophen-induced acute liver damage by inhibiting oxidative stress through activation of the Keap1/Nrf2/HO-1 signaling pathway.
Pretreatment with BKA mitigates liver injury and improves CYP2E1 expression in mouse livers.

entries.title: Signaling Pathways in Inflammation and Anti-inflammatory Therapies.

sentences: Among genes with available literature context, Stat3 has been extensively characterized as a mediator of cytokine signaling, inflammatory responses, and cardiac stress adaptation [40, 41], and its potential involvement in the cardiac transcriptional response to 1,2-DCB would be consistent with known roles in heart-liver cross-talk following myocardial stress [41].

statements: Inflammation plays a critical role in chronic diseases such as neurodegeneration, cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and inflammatory bowel disease.
The p38 MAPK, IL-6/JAK/STAT3, PI3K pathways and the Hippo pathway are associated with inflammation initiation and progression.

sentences: Sod2, encoding manganese superoxide dismutase, is a well-established marker of mitochondrial oxidative stress and has been reported to be regulated through Nrf2 and related antioxidant pathways in multiple organ systems [42, 43, 44]; its presence among the responsive genes would support an oxidative stress component to the cardiac response.

entries.title: Klotho ameliorates diabetic nephropathy by activating Nrf2 signaling pathway in podocytes.

entries.title: Nrf2/ARE is a key pathway for curcumin-mediated protection of TMJ chondrocytes from oxidative stress and inflammation

sentences: Sod2, encoding manganese superoxide dismutase, is a well-established marker of mitochondrial oxidative stress and has been reported to be regulated through Nrf2 and related antioxidant pathways in multiple organ systems [42, 43, 44]; its presence among the responsive genes would support an oxidative stress component to the cardiac response.

statements: Curcumin inhibits inflammation and oxidative stress in TMJ chondrocytes through activation of the Nrf2/ARE pathway.
Curcumin upregulates cartilage anabolic factors COL2A1 and ACAN while downregulating matrix-degrading proteinases MMPs and ADAMTSs.
Specific inhibition of Nrf2 abrogates curcumin-induced anti-inflammatory effects in TMJ chondrocytes.
